A photorealistic wide, downward-looking picture of a cramped, cheap basement gym in a small English town, taken from a fixed point high in one corner of the ceiling, close to the wall, as if a small unattended camera were bolted up there and nobody was behind it. Nothing is framed for effect: the bench press sits slightly off to the left, a rack of mismatched rubber-coated dumbbells and a cracked mirror fill the right, and the floor is scuffed black rubber matting with a bald patch near the door. On the bench lies a gangly young man with a long pale face, a weak chin, a patchy ginger-brown beard that has not decided to grow, narrow sloping shoulders and a washed-out grey hoodie rolled up to his elbows, straining under a bar loaded with thin plates and shaking visibly. Standing over his head, spotting him, is a heavy-set older man with a shaved head, thick grey stubble, a sunburnt neck, a belly pushing out a faded navy vest, and the tired, patient expression of someone who has watched this go wrong before. Both are small in the frame, seen from above and slightly to the side, their faces tilted and partly foreshortened. The only light is two flickering tube lights in the ceiling, giving a flat greenish-white wash, with a dim doorway of daylight at the far end that burns out to pale white. The picture is soft and slightly smeared, low in resolution, with faded washed-out colour, muted greens and greys, visible noise in the shadows and gently bowed edges from a cheap wide lens, filling the whole frame edge to edge with only the room itself in view. Thanks.

A photorealistic picture of a rented attic bedroom at night, seen from a laptop left open and propped on a rumpled duvet at the foot of a single bed, so the lens looks slightly up and across at the room, close to the floor and tilted a few degrees off level. A very thin young man with a round, doughy, spotty face, small close-set eyes, big ears, a scrubby neck beard and uncombed black hair is on his back on a bare patch of carpet between the bed and a sloping roof beam, hands clasped behind his head, in the middle of a crunch, face screwed up with effort. He wears a huge stained charcoal hoodie, grey jogging bottoms gone shiny at the knees and one white sock with a hole in the heel. His phone lies on the carpet beside his head and is the main light: a cold blue-white glow from below that lights his chin, nostrils and the underside of the sloping ceiling, and leaves the rest of the attic in deep murk. Around him are a heap of unwashed clothes, a mug with a skin of something in it, a bare mattress edge, a clothes rail bowed under hoodies, and a small dormer window showing a dull orange streetlight smear. The picture is dark and grainy as if the camera is struggling in low light, with crushed shadows, smudged detail, slightly blown highlights where the phone glows, washed-out colour and a faint softness, and it fills the whole frame edge to edge with only the room and the people in it. Thanks.

A photorealistic wide picture of the inside of a parked ambulance's patient bay, taken from a small fixed lens tucked into the ceiling corner above the rear doors, looking down the length of the compartment, with nobody operating it and no movement in the framing. The curved wall is lined with cupboards of grey plastic, a strapped-in oxygen cylinder and a pale yellow sharps bin. On the stretcher lies a skinny young man with a narrow lopsided face, a broken-looking nose, bad skin on his forehead, pale eyebrows and a flat blond fringe stuck down with sweat, wearing a thin white t-shirt and one trainer. His right arm lies across his chest wrapped in an enormous lumpy mess of white medical tape and a sagging crepe bandage, fingers poking out puffy and purple, and in his other hand he gripping a plain unmarked plastic shaker bottle of chalky beige liquid, looking at it with a mixture of pride and shame. Seated beside him on a fold-down seat is a stocky woman paramedic in her thirties with a square freckled face, a short practical brown ponytail, wide set tired eyes and a green uniform with the sleeves pushed up, one gloved hand on his wrist, her mouth set in flat disbelief. Both are seen from above and foreshortened, small in the picture. The only light is a hard, cold white strip across the ceiling that makes the steel and plastic shine, with the street outside turning the rear window into a pale blur. The picture is slightly soft, faded and low in resolution, with muted greens and greyish whites, noise in the corners and gentle bowing at the edges from a cheap wide lens, filling the whole frame edge to edge with only the vehicle interior in view. Thanks.

A photorealistic, slightly washed-out frame from the front camera of a phone propped against a stack of paperbacks on a shelf in a rented attic room, the picture soft and a little grainy as a cheap lens gives it, the image filling the whole frame edge to edge with nothing laid over it. Brandon, 22, a skinny underfed young man with a narrow, very pale face, a scatter of angry red spots across his forehead and chin, thin cracked lips, sunken cheeks and ears that stick out like open car doors, mousy hair flattened on one side from the pillow. He sits cross-legged on a bare single mattress in a faded oversized grey hoodie with frayed cuffs, wrists like sticks, looking at the lens with a hopeful, blank stare, mouth slightly open as if mid-sentence. The only light is the glow of the phone screen on his face from below, mixing with a dim orange bulb out of frame, so his skin looks greenish-white and the sloping attic ceiling behind him falls into murky shadow. Visible pores, shiny oily patches at the nose, dry flaking skin by one eyebrow, mismatched cheap bedding and a damp patch on the plaster behind him. Thanks.

A photorealistic, murky still as seen by the lens of a phone leaning on a windowsill in a cramped English attic bedroom, the picture slightly overexposed where daylight leaks in and muddy everywhere else, shown as a plain full-bleed photograph with nothing drawn on top of it. Brandon, 22, a soft, pudgy young man with a round moon face, a double chin starting, patchy ginger-brown stubble that grows in clumps and leaves bare gaps along the jaw, and a hairline already retreating at the temples with thin hair combed forward over the forehead. He sits slumped at a wobbly desk in a stretched navy tracksuit top, crumbs on the chest, leaning close to the lens so his face fills much of the frame, eyebrows raised in earnest worry, a little sweat on the upper lip. Pale flat daylight from a grubby skylight above and behind him blows out the edge of the picture, and a cold blue cast from the screen he is reading lights the front of his face. Pink flushed cheeks, creased eyelids, slightly chapped skin, a mug ringed with tea stains and a heap of clothes on a chair behind him. Thanks.

A photorealistic still from the front camera of a phone wedged into the gap of a wardrobe door in a rented attic, the lens close and slightly wide so the face stretches a touch at the edges, picture noisy and dim like a phone in a poorly lit room, the whole frame clean photograph with nothing overlaid. Brandon, 22, a gangly young man with a long horse-like face, a pronounced overbite that keeps his front teeth resting on his lower lip, a prominent Adam's apple, and a home-bleached fringe that has turned a brassy, patchy orange with darker brown roots showing at the parting. He is crouched forward on the edge of a sagging bed in a thin black t-shirt with a cracked print, long collarbones, knobbly shoulders, eyes wide and a little too intense, mid-grin, head tilted toward the lens. Light comes from one bare bulb on a flex hanging off-centre above him, throwing hard shadows under his brow and nose, plus a faint blue flicker from the screen. Chemical-damaged straw-like hair, a pink scalp patch where the bleach burned, a few stubble hairs on a narrow chin, fading yellow bruise on one forearm, peeling wallpaper behind. Thanks.

A photorealistic still in the manner of a phone's front camera, the phone balanced on a pile of cardboard boxes at the end of a rented attic room, picture a bit compressed and warm-greyed, with one side of the frame lit brighter than the other, delivered as a clean full-frame photograph with nothing placed over it. Brandon, 22, a short, stocky, broad-chested mixed-race British young man with warm light-brown skin, a thick neck, deep acne scars pitting both cheeks and the jaw, and a terrible home clipper job: uneven patches of fuzz, a stripe shaved too close above the left ear, a ragged step at the crown. His dark eyes are bright and very eager, eyebrows lifted, a big hopeful half-smile showing slightly crooked teeth, face pushed a little too close to the lens. He wears a tight, bobbled burgundy jumper with one sleeve pushed up over a thick forearm. Weak grey daylight comes from a small roof window to his right, with a yellow lamp low on the left, so one cheek is cool and the other warm and the scarring catches the light. Faint sheen on the forehead, ingrown stubble on the chin, a tiny scab near his hairline, a drying rack of grey socks behind his shoulder. Thanks.

A photorealistic still of a heavy-set, slouching man with a wide soft face, a pale bald crown ringed by thin grey stubble, deep lines from nose to mouth, loose jowls and tired, pouched eyes that are slightly bloodshot. He wears a washed-out grey cotton vest that sags at the neck and shows pink sunburnt shoulders and freckled forearms. He has stopped directly beneath a camera fixed high in the corner of a municipal gym and glanced up and back over his shoulder, his chin tilted up so the lens looks down on his scalp and brow, his expression flat and unhappy as he checks the room. Behind him are rubber floor tiles, a rack of chipped black dumbbells and a pale breeze-block wall. The only light is a flat, greenish strip light directly overhead that leaves shadow in his eye sockets and under his chin. The picture is soft, slightly smeared and low in contrast, with muted colour and fine digital noise, as if a cheap fixed camera had recorded it unattended. Entirely clean frame with no overlay, lettering or numerals of any kind. Thanks.

A photorealistic still of a thin, sinewy man with a long narrow face, hollow cheeks, a sharp Adam's apple and a drooping moustache stained nicotine-yellow at the middle, a few fair eyebrow hairs, and watery pale-blue eyes with heavy bags. His thin hair is combed over in oily strands. He wears a bobbled navy fleece with a faded embroidered patch on the chest that is too blurred to read, zipped up to the throat. He has walked right up under a camera mounted near the ceiling of a gym and glanced up at it with a weary squint, one hand rubbing the back of his neck while he checks the room behind him. We see him from slightly above, steeply foreshortened, with his forehead large and his chin small. Behind him are mirrored panels smeared with fingerprints and a row of cross-trainers. A single fluorescent tube overhead gives a cold, uneven light and a window on the far side is blown out to white. The image is soft and washed out with coarse grain and slightly crushed shadows, the look of footage from an unattended wide-angle camera. No writing, symbols or graphics appear anywhere in the frame. Thanks.

A photorealistic still of a Black British man with a broad forehead, deep-set heavy-lidded eyes with dark, puffy undereyes, a full beard going grey in patches at the chin and cheeks, a grey-flecked close-cropped head and a slightly rounded, tired face with a scar through the left eyebrow. He wears a black polyester zip-up tracksuit top with its zip pulled halfway, over a crumpled white T-shirt. He has stopped just under a ceiling-corner camera in a community leisure-centre gym and tilted his head up to glance at it, his mouth slack and his gaze weary and watchful, one shoulder turned towards the door he has just checked. The view is from high above and a little to the side, so we see the crown of his head, the top of his nose and his beard. Behind him are blue exercise mats stacked against a wall, a dented water fountain and a scuffed double door. Light comes from a row of ceiling panels that flicker slightly and cast flat, shadowless illumination, with a cold bright window at the edge of the frame. The picture is slightly muddy and compressed, with dulled colour and visible grain, as from a fixed unattended camera. The frame is bare picture only: no text, numbers or interface graphics. Thanks.

A photorealistic still of a soft-bodied man with heavy jowls, a thick neck, a nose that was broken once and sits crooked with a flattened bridge, small close-set brown eyes under a creased brow, a high receding hairline with wispy dark hair above the ears, and blotchy red cheeks with broken veins. He wears a faded, thin cotton T-shirt in washed-out orange from an old charity fun run, its printing cracked and illegible, stretched over his belly and with a small stain near the hem. He has walked underneath a camera bolted high in the corner of a gym and glanced up at it with a tired, sidelong look, mouth slightly open, one eyebrow lowered as he checks the room. We look down at him from above, so his forehead and receding hair dominate and his chin doubles. Behind him are a treadmill, a scuffed wall of peeling green paint and a stack of grubby yoga blocks. A hard overhead tube light puts dark shadows under his brow and nose, and a dirty skylight smears pale daylight across one side of the floor. The image is slightly soft and bleached with fine noise and flattened colour, as if captured by a fixed lens that nobody operates. Nothing is written or drawn over the picture: no characters, no marks, no interface. Thanks.

A still from a laptop's built-in webcam during a work video call, the picture soft, blocky and smeared by heavy compression, with the colours slightly washed out and the shadows turning to mud. The camera sits low and a little crooked on a desk, looking up and slightly tilted at a tanned, broad-faced man in his early fifties with a deep orange-brown tan that stops abruptly at a pale band along his hairline, creased squint lines, a high shiny forehead, thin sandy-grey hair combed into a neat side parting, a soft rounded jaw with a little loose skin under it, and small bright pleased-with-himself eyes that are looking at something off the edge of the screen, not at the lens. He wears a navy quilted gilet zipped up over a pale blue open-collared shirt, and he is chewing a mouthful of salad from a clear plastic supermarket tub held near his chin, a fork hovering, a leaf of rocket stuck to the fork. Behind him is a dark wooden bookcase crammed with unevenly stacked hardbacks and a framed photo of a sailing boat, its books too blurred and blocky to read. The only light is a flat cool glow from the laptop screen on his face and a bright overexposed window to one side that blows out the edge of the frame. Nothing is written on the picture anywhere: no text, no numbers, no icons, no borders, just the raw picture. Thanks.

A blurry, over-compressed frame from a laptop webcam on a video call, a little pixelated, with a greenish-grey cast and flat dull light from a ceiling lamp out of shot. A narrow, long-faced bald man in his late forties sits very upright and close to the camera, so his head fills the middle of the frame and the top is slightly cut off. His scalp is pale and faintly shiny with a few freckles, his eyebrows are thin and almost invisible, his cheeks are hollow with a pinched, slightly sour mouth, a long nose, and a blotchy shaving rash on his neck. He wears rimless glasses that catch two small glare spots from the screen, and a pewter-grey fleece-lined gilet over a white shirt with the collar buttoned too high. He is forking limp lettuce and a few cherry tomatoes out of a Tupperware box with his eyes drifting to the side, plainly reading something else, jaw working slowly. Behind him is a bare white wall with one tall artificial pot plant with glossy dust-covered leaves in the right corner and nothing else at all. The picture has no writing, numbers, symbols or overlays of any kind, only the plain webcam image. Thanks.

A still from a cheap laptop webcam during a video call, smeared and blocky with compression, the highlights glowing and the colours slightly oversaturated and smudged, as if the signal were struggling. The camera is propped on a kitchen island and looks up the man's chin. He is a heavy, big-framed man in his late thirties with a ruddy, windburnt, red-veined face, broken capillaries across his round cheeks and nose, a double chin, a thick neck, small pale blue eyes under sandy eyebrows, and a thick floppy fringe of dirty-blond hair falling across his forehead and sticking up at the back. He wears a bottle-green quilted gilet over a rumpled pink checked shirt with the sleeves pushed up his thick forearms. He is hunched over a large wooden bowl of salad, shovelling a forkful in while his eyes slide off to one side, half asleep with boredom. Behind him is a big new kitchen extension: a pale grey island unit, glass bi-fold doors onto a lawn in flat white daylight that burns out the glass, a row of copper pans hung in a line. The only light is the daylight behind him and the pale screen glow in front. No text, numbers, icons, borders or interface appear anywhere on the picture, which is just the raw image. Thanks.

A small, wiry woman of about forty-five stands on her own front step, close to the door, staring straight into a tiny wide lens mounted in the door frame at chest height, because she has just noticed it and is deciding what to say to it. She has a narrow, sharp-boned face with a pointed chin, pale skin with fine lines at the eyes and mouth, thin dry lips pressed together, and one eyebrow slightly raised. Her short hair is cropped and uneven, dark brown with wide grey streaks over the temples. A pair of reading glasses hangs on a faded green cord against a bobbled charcoal jumper, and one hand holds a rolled-up bundle of leaflets and a pen. The picture is the flat, slightly bowed view of a cheap wide lens looking down at her from above: her head looks a touch large, her shoulders sloped, the red brick porch and a wheelie bin curving at the edges. It is a grey damp English afternoon, soft overcast daylight with the sky behind her blown out to white, colours washed and slightly muddy, soft compressed detail and a little noise in the shadows. Nothing is written or drawn over the image: it is only the raw picture itself, with no lettering, digits, icons or frame furniture. Thanks.

A tired British Asian woman in her late thirties stands at her front door at dusk and looks directly into the small wide lens set into the door frame above her, her head tilted a few degrees and her mouth flat, caught mid-thought as she realises it is watching her. She has a round, soft, slightly puffy face, warm brown skin with dark smudges under the eyes and a few spots along the jaw, thick straight black eyebrows, and a faint crease between them. Her long black hair is pulled into a loose, low knot with strands escaping across one cheek. She wears an oatmeal knitted cardigan, pilled at the elbows, over a creased blue shirt, and a council lanyard in a washed-out teal hangs round her neck with a laminated card turned face-in so nothing on it can be read; she holds a carrier bag of shopping and a set of keys. The view is steeply from above through a cheap lens, so the edges of the porch bow inward and her feet feel far away. The only light is a yellow street lamp from the left and a hallway bulb leaking round the door behind her, so her face is half orange and half grey-blue, the dark parts crushed and grainy, colours drained and smeared by heavy compression. The frame holds only the scene itself, with no writing, numbers, symbols or overlays of any kind. Thanks.

A big, broad woman of about fifty-five stands square in front of her door on a freezing morning and stares straight up into the small wide lens set in the door frame, chin lifted, one eyebrow down, having obviously spotted it and taken it personally. She is tall and heavy-set with wide shoulders and a thick neck. Her large round face is flushed raw red from the cold across the cheeks and nose, thickly freckled over pale skin, with broken veins at the nostrils, a double chin, deep lines either side of a wide mouth, and chapped lips. Her ginger hair has faded to sandy and white at the front and is flattened under a hairband that she has pushed back, leaving a frizz of loose wisps. She wears an old, bobbled forest-green walking fleece with a zip pulled up to the chin and a sagging collar, a rip at one cuff mended with black thread, and muddy boots with the laces undone. The picture comes from above through a cheap lens, so she looms and the porch tiles curve away. Low winter sun from behind the camera side glares off her wet face and the white painted door; frost sits on a doormat, the whites are clipped, the colour is thin and chalky, and fine noise crawls in the dark areas. There is nothing written, drawn or displayed on the image, no letters, numbers or interface; it is only the picture. Thanks.

A photorealistic still of a stocky paramedic in her early thirties, seen from above and slightly to one side, looking straight up into the lens as she reaches overhead for something on a shelf in the back of an ambulance. Her face is broad and round, with a heavy jaw, a flat freckled nose, small pale-lashed grey eyes, chapped lips and a faint red mark across the bridge of the nose where a mask has sat for too many hours. Her hair is cropped close to the skull in uneven sandy-brown clippers work, with a few grey strands at the temple. She wears a green paramedic jacket with a frayed collar over a creased green uniform shirt; her sleeve is pushed to the elbow and her raised forearm carries a faded blue-black tattoo of a swallow above a ribbon of illegible script, the ink blurred with age. Her shoulders are thick and slumped with tiredness. The camera is a fixed unmanned lens bolted high in the ceiling corner of the vehicle, so the picture is wide, slightly distorted at the edges, a little soft, washed-out and flat in colour, with fine night-time grain and slightly crushed shadows. The only light is one long cold fluorescent strip along the ceiling, which flattens her face and leaves pale glare on the steel cabinets, blue-grey rubber flooring, a folded red blanket, a stretcher with a scuffed mattress and a dented oxygen cylinder. The picture contains no words, numbers, symbols, borders or overlays of any kind, only the scene itself. Thanks.

A photorealistic still of a Black British paramedic in her late twenties, looking up into the lens with a tired, crooked, kind smile while she stretches one arm up towards a high compartment inside an ambulance. Her face is oval with a high forehead, full cheeks, deep brown skin that shows a little shine on the nose and forehead, a small scar through her left eyebrow, slightly puffy lids, and a gap between her front teeth. Her long box braids are twisted up into a lopsided knot on top of her head, with a few loose strands stuck to her neck. She wears a dark green uniform jacket zipped halfway over a grey fleece, a lanyard with a clutch of keys, and blue nitrile gloves, one of them with a torn fingertip. The camera is a fixed, unattended lens up in the corner of the ceiling, looking down across the length of the cabin, so she is small in the frame, the angle is steep, and the colours are drained and compressed like an old webcam picture, with soft detail and mild noise. The only light is a single hard strip light overhead, giving her a pale glare on the forehead and deep shadow under the chin, with a little orange streetlamp glow leaking in through the frosted rear window. Around her are a battered grab bag, tangled blue tubing, a roll of paper towel and a tipped-over paper coffee cup on a bench. The picture contains no words, numbers, symbols, borders or overlays of any kind, only the scene itself. Thanks.

A photorealistic still of a very tall, thin paramedic woman in her mid thirties, stooped under the low roof of an ambulance cabin, craning her head back to look up into the lens as she reaches up for a box on a high rack. Her face is long and narrow, with sunken cheeks, deep violet-brown hollows under pale hazel eyes, thin lips, a pointed chin and a nose that has clearly been broken: bent to the right at the bridge with a bump halfway down. Her skin is sallow and uneven with dry patches by the nostrils. Her mousy brown hair is pulled back in a thin, greasy ponytail, with flyaways falling across her brow. Her wrists stick out of sleeves that are too short on a faded green uniform shirt with a pen clipped to the pocket and a coffee stain on the hem, and her long hand is spread open as it reaches. The camera is a fixed, operator-less lens in a ceiling corner of the vehicle, looking down at her from above, so her height is squashed, the wide picture bends slightly at the edges, the colour is faded and grey-green, and the image is grainy and low in contrast, like footage that nobody expected to watch. The only light is one pale strip tube above her and a faint blue flicker from a monitor out of sight, which leaves her eye sockets in shadow. Around her are a stretcher with a crumpled sheet, a yellow sharps bin, a stack of clipboards and a muddy boot print on the floor. The picture contains no words, numbers, symbols, borders or overlays of any kind, only the scene itself. Thanks.
